title: Bridge and Lantern
premise: In the winter of 1899, during a colonial border war, Ivo Okafor works as a battlefield nurse at a river garrison, secretly recording in his ledger the names of soldiers whose deaths officers erase to protect reputations and pensions. When a stranger arrives bearing letters in the handwriting of Captain Aldous Vane — officially dead for two years and quietly responsible for a massacre being buried by the same men Ivo serves — Ivo realizes his ledger is not just memory but evidence. To carry it past three military checkpoints before New Year's Day, when the century turns and all garrison records are burned, Ivo must ally with the stranger, who may be Vane himself wearing another man's name. At the final checkpoint Ivo trades his own safety for the ledger's passage, mailing it to a London journalist as he is arrested; an epilogue reveals the names published years later, his handwriting preserved in the trial record.
about_author: Lior Marchetti is the pen name of a former field medic turned archivist who spent a decade cataloguing colonial-era hospital records in West African and Caribbean repositories. Bridge and Lantern is their first novel, drawn from marginalia found in a genuine casualty ledger.

chapters.title: The Ledger of Small Names
chapters.summary: Ivo's POV. At the River Sante garrison hospital, Ivo tends wounded soldiers and records in a hidden notebook the names officers strike from official rolls. The emotional beat is quiet defiance: he cannot stop the dying, but he can refuse the forgetting.

chapters.title: What the Colonel Signs
chapters.summary: Ivo's POV. Colonel Brase delivers a speech honoring fallen men whose bodies were never recovered; Ivo recognizes three of them alive in his ward last month. He begins copying orders that pass through the infirmary. The beat is dawning suspicion hardening into purpose.

chapters.title: A Stranger at the Ford
chapters.summary: Ivo's POV. A half-frozen traveler, calling himself Mr. Pell, collapses at the bridge checkpoint and is brought in feverish. In his satchel Ivo glimpses letters signed A. Vane — the dead captain's unmistakable looping hand. The beat is electric unease.

chapters.title: The Hand of a Dead Man
chapters.summary: Ivo's POV, with a flashback to Vane's alleged death two years prior. Ivo confronts the sleeping Pell, who wakes lucid and says only: 'You keep lists too.' The beat is recognition between two people hiding the same secret from opposite sides.

chapters.title: Pell's Account
chapters.summary: Pell's POV. He claims to be Vane's former clerk, sent to deliver proof of the Kessari Crossing massacre to a journalist before records burn on January 1st. Ivo tests the story against his own ledger entries. The beat is reluctant alliance built on mutual blackmail potential.

chapters.title: Three Checkpoints
chapters.summary: Ivo's POV. They map the route: the bridge guard, the rail depot at Marrow Junction, and the coastal customs house. Each requires papers neither fully possesses. The beat is cold planning, tension braided with growing trust.

chapters.title: Sister Amara Notices
chapters.summary: Amara's POV. Head nurse Amara catches Ivo copying documents and, instead of reporting him, reveals she lost a brother at Kessari Crossing. She joins them but warns that Sergeant Doyle suspects the stranger. The beat is grief converted into solidarity.

chapters.title: Doyle's Questions
chapters.summary: Ivo's POV. Sergeant Doyle searches the infirmary under pretext of a supply audit; Ivo hides the ledger inside a corpse's shroud. The near-discovery leaves him shaking. The beat is terror sharpening his resolve — survival now requires risk.

chapters.title: The Colonel's Dinner
chapters.summary: Ivo's POV. Summoned to serve at Brase's table, Ivo hears officers toast the century's end and joke about burning 'the old paper shame' with it. He learns the burn order includes private correspondence. The beat is quiet horror: even memory itself is scheduled for destruction.

chapters.title: Vane's Letters
chapters.summary: Pell's POV. Reading the letters aloud by lamplight, they reconstruct the massacre: Vane ordered it, then was allowed to vanish rather than face court-martial, protected by Brase. One letter mentions 'the nurse who writes things down.' The beat is dread — someone has been watching Ivo.

chapters.title: First Checkpoint: The Bridge
chapters.summary: Ivo's POV. Disguised as a medical supply run, Pell crosses the bridge using forged papers while Ivo creates a diversion with a staged emergency. It works, barely. The beat is exhilaration curdling into guilt over the orderly injured in the diversion.

chapters.title: The Price of the Diversion
chapters.summary: Ivo's POV. The injured orderly, young Ferro, asks Ivo directly whether he caused the accident. Ivo lies, then writes Ferro's name in the ledger anyway — the first living name. The beat is moral corrosion: survival is costing him the very integrity the ledger represents.

chapters.title: Marrow Junction
chapters.summary: Pell's POV. At the rail depot, Doyle appears unexpectedly, transferred ahead of them. Pell must board the same train as his hunter. The beat is claustrophobic suspense across a night journey, the ledger sewn into Pell's coat lining.

chapters.title: Night Train Confessions
chapters.summary: Pell's POV. Cornered in the smoking car, Pell tells Doyle a partial truth — that he carries Vane's confession — offering to share the blame. Doyle hesitates, revealing his own brother died at Kessari. The beat is dangerous ambiguity: enemy or ally?

chapters.title: Betrayal at Dawn
chapters.summary: Ivo's POV. Word reaches the garrison that Pell was taken at Marrow Junction. Amara urges Ivo to burn the ledger and survive; he refuses. The beat is despair met with stubbornness — the book must reach the coast even if no one does.

chapters.title: Second Checkpoint: Alone
chapters.summary: Ivo's POV. Ivo travels the rail route himself carrying a duplicate ledger, leaving the true one hidden in Amara's care. At the depot he passes inspection by impersonating a dead officer's aide — using a name from his own list. The beat is eerie self-erasure: becoming one of the forgotten to save them.

chapters.title: Doyle's Choice
chapters.summary: Doyle's POV. Interrogating Pell, Doyle finds the duplicate ledger planted on him and realizes Ivo used them both. Facing his brother's ghost, Doyle lets Pell escape the cell and reports the ledger 'destroyed.' The beat is redemption purchased with treason.

chapters.title: Third Checkpoint: The Customs House
chapters.summary: Ivo's POV. At the coast, the customs officer demands to open every parcel. Ivo mails the pages individually inside medicine envelopes addressed to a London journal, keeping only the cover blank. The beat is agonizing patience as each envelope disappears into the mailbag.

chapters.title: The Century Turns
chapters.summary: Ivo's POV. On New Year's Eve, garrison fires consume the old records while church bells ring in 1900. Brase, promoted, thanks Ivo publicly for his service. The beat is bitter irony — honored by the man he is destroying.

chapters.title: Arrest at the Lantern Bridge
chapters.summary: Ivo's POV. Doyle, ordered to arrest Ivo after all, finds him waiting on the bridge. Ivo offers no resistance, asking only that the lantern be left lit for the ferryman. The beat is calm acceptance; he has already won and knows it.

chapters.title: The Trial of Paper
chapters.summary: Amara's POV, months later. In a military courtroom, the published ledger pages are entered as evidence; Brase falls, Vane is extradited, and Ivo — sentenced to two years — listens as clerks read his own handwriting aloud. The beat is vindication shadowed by cost.

chapters.title: Every Name Read Aloud
chapters.summary: Ivo's POV, epilogue, 1904. Released, Ivo visits the rebuilt bridge where a small plaque bears no names — deliberately. Instead, children recite the ledger's names each year by lantern light. He adds Ferro's name, still living, and closes the book. The beat is peace: memory outlived power.
